sources.title: Researchers explore the use of AI and smart sensors to improve food safety quickly, affordably

en.title: Researchers develop AI-powered sensor to detect food allergens quickly and affordably
en.dek: A new prototype uses near-infrared spectroscopy and artificial intelligence to identify allergenic proteins in food without destroying samples.
facts: The smartJAN project developed a functional prototype that detects lipid transfer proteins (LTPs), plant allergens linked to severe reactions.
The technology combines near-infrared spectroscopy with AI algorithms to analyze how light reflects off food, creating a spectral 'fingerprint'.
Tested allergens include Pru p 3 from peach skin and Ara h 9 from peanuts, both studied as part of the project.
The system has previously demonstrated effectiveness in detecting gluten and bacteria such as Salmonella in meat.
The prototype is designed for integration into food industry quality control, not for consumer or domestic use.
body: Researchers from the University of Deusto, in collaboration with Kernet and Fundación Miranda, have completed development of a functional prototype that detects allergenic lipid transfer proteins in food. The smartJAN project combines near-infrared spectroscopy with signal-processing algorithms and artificial intelligence to analyze how light reflects off a food sample, producing a spectral 'fingerprint' that the AI system interprets instantly. The work, published in the journal Food Analytical Methods, tested the technology on allergens such as Pru p 3 from peach skin and Ara h 9 from peanuts.

Begoña García-Zapirain, head of the eVIDA research group, noted that the technology could have wider applications beyond the initial study. Previous tests have demonstrated the system's effectiveness in detecting gluten and the presence of bacteria in meat, suggesting it could pave the way for early detection of pathogens that cause food poisoning. The initiative specifically targeted allergenic proteins from the LTP family, which are particularly relevant in the Mediterranean region.

Once protocols for validating its reliability are completed, the speed of the analysis could facilitate food screening and complement conventional analytical methods, helping to speed up quality control procedures in the food industry and distribution chains. The device is not intended for end consumers or domestic use but rather for integration into quality control processes in institutional catering facilities and the food industry. With the research phase now complete, the next step toward bringing this tool to market will depend on industrial interest in turning the prototype into a commercially available testing device.
en.context: Food allergen detection traditionally requires laboratory testing, which can be time-consuming and expensive. This new technology aims to provide a faster, more affordable method for identifying specific allergens in the food production chain.
